Seafood / Contemporary

Doenjang-Butter Grilled Scallops

Grilled scallops with a contemporary pairing of butter and fermented soybean paste.

Korean · Easy · Serves 3–4 (makes 12)

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 02 / 15 seafood recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: contemporary — the fusion seat, labeled honestly. Doenjang and butter is the modern Korean bistro's signature move, and scallops are its best argument: the paste's fermented depth against sweet shellfish richness, with butter carrying both. Nothing about this record claims a lineage — it is exactly what its label says, a contemporary build using the pantry's oldest paste — and it is on the site because it is delicious and because it teaches the doenjang-and-fat principle better than any stew does.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Buy dry-packed scallops and dry them further. Wet scallops (soaked in phosphate solution) never sear — they leach white liquid into the pan and steam in it. Dry-packed, patted down, and left air-drying on paper towel for 10 minutes while the grill heats: that is the sear's whole foundation.
  • Whisk the baste warm: butter melted, doenjang worked in until smooth (a small bowl and a fork, one minute), honey, garlic, sesame oil. It should taste intensely savory-salty-buttery — it is a glaze in search of sweetness, which is what the scallop supplies.
  • Fire at medium-high with a flat cast-iron surface or grate bars wiped with oil — scallops need full contact, not grates with gaps.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Sear dry scallops, undisturbed, 90 seconds — no baste yet, because butter burns where the paste would scorch. The sear happens in plain fat and the flavor comes after. Checkpoint — lift one: a deep golden-brown crust on the bottom face. No crust, back down — and if the pan was smoking hard, it ran a notch hot for butter's tolerance.
  2. 02
    Flip, and baste the seared faces now — brush or spoon the doenjang-butter over each scallop, 60–90 seconds more, off the fire while the centers still carry the faintest translucence at the very core (carryover finishes them on the platter). Checkpoint — the basted tops should sit glossy and foamy-gold. A test scallop cut in half: opaque to within a few millimeters of the center, buttery, just springy. Fully opaque-through at the pan means slightly over — edible, but the next batch pulls 15 seconds sooner.
  3. 03
    Flaky salt, scallion, sesame; serve immediately, off the shared platter, one or two per diner with rice beside. Checkpoint — eating test: crust, then the sweet scallop burst, then doenjang's savory depth arriving on the butter — the three arriving in that order is the build working. Salty-only means the baste ran heavy on paste; a teaspoon, not a tablespoon, is the ratio. Chef’s Note — the phosphate scallop warning is the record's most practical paragraph: "wet" scallops say dry-packed's opposite nowhere on the label — you recognize them by the milk-white liquid they weep in the pan and a soapy-sweet flavor that no sear fixes. Buy from a fish counter you trust, ask for dry-packed, and if the only option is wet, skip this record and make #SF02's shrimp instead — the failure mode is not survivable.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
White liquid flooding the panPhosphate-soaked scallopsBuy dry-packed; next time ask the counter
No crust, gray searWet surface or lukew panBone-dry scallops; preheat fully
Baste burnt bitterBasted too earlyPlain-fat sear first, baste after the flip
Salty over-sweet meatBaste too thickOne brush-stroke per scallop; a teaspoon of paste per 12

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Scallops are cook-and-eat; raw ones keep 24 hours on ice in the fridge, no marinade. The baste keeps a week refrigerated and improves.
  • Variations: a drop of gochujang into the baste for heat; the same baste on king oyster mushroom slices for the table's vegetarians; stirred into rice at the end — the leftover baste's best job.
